title: The pH scale, stomach acid and antacids: why does the burning go away?

summary.text: After a heavy feast, some grown-ups feel a burning in the chest. They chew a chalky tablet, and the burning fades in minutes. The tablet is a base, and it is fighting an acid that the stomach makes on purpose. Your child races different powders against a glass of acid, counts how many scoops each one needs, and learns what the numbers on the pH scale really mean. They find out why every step on the scale is ten times bigger than the last, and why the stomach does not burn itself. They also meet the two doctors who proved that a bacterium can live in stomach acid.
summary.art: A glass of pink cabbage-water acid with a hand adding a scoop of white powder, and the colour turning purple in a row of four glasses beside it.

intro.hook: After a big wedding feast, a grown-up chews a white tablet, and the burning in their chest goes away within minutes. The tablet never touched the burn. So what did it do?
intro.text: A burning in the chest after a meal is called heartburn. It has nothing to do with the heart. Acid from the stomach has splashed up into the food pipe, and the food pipe has no shield against it. A tablet that stops the burning must change that acid. In this unit you make a glass of 'stomach acid' with vinegar and cabbage water. Then you race different powders to see which one beats it. You also learn to read the pH scale with real numbers, and you find out why the stomach does not burn itself.
intro.art: A grown-up at a wedding feast table with a banana-leaf plate, holding a hand to the chest and chewing a white tablet, with a glass of water nearby.

outcomes: I can read the pH scale from 0 to 14 and say whether a number means an acid, neutral or a base.
I can explain that each step on the pH scale is ten times bigger than the last, and work out how many times more acidic one liquid is than another.
I can use an indicator, such as cabbage water or pH paper, to place a liquid on the pH scale, and say how rough or exact the reading is.
I can explain why the stomach makes a strong acid, and how its lining keeps itself safe from it.
I can explain how an antacid works, and run a fair test that counts how much of each powder it takes to neutralise the same acid.
I can explain why too much base is as wrong as too much acid, and why the body keeps different places at different pH.
I can tell how Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that a bacterium lives in the stomach and causes most ulcers.

terms.meaning: A number that says how acidic or basic a watery liquid is. A low number means a strong acid. A high number means a strong base. Seven is neutral.
terms.example: Lemon juice is about pH 2. Pure water is pH 7. Soapy water is about pH 9.
terms.art: A long strip from 0 to 14 with a lemon at 2, a glass of water at 7 and a bar of soap at 9.

terms.meaning: A tiny hydrogen particle that carries an electric charge and floats free in a watery liquid. The more hydrogen ions a liquid has, the more acidic it is.
terms.example: Lemon juice holds about 100,000 times more hydrogen ions than pure water.
terms.art: A glass of lemon juice zoomed in to show many small particles marked H plus, and a glass of water zoomed in to show very few.

terms.meaning: Ten times as much. A tenfold step multiplies a number by ten.
terms.example: A drop of dye in ten spoons of water is a tenfold dilution. The colour is ten times weaker.
terms.art: Three glasses in a row, each with a colour ten times paler than the one before.

terms.meaning: A dye that changes colour to show how acidic or basic a liquid is.
terms.example: Red cabbage water is pink in acid and green in a strong base.
terms.art: Three glasses of cabbage water in pink, purple and green with a lemon, a glass of water and a bar of soap beside them.

terms.meaning: A mixture of several dyes that gives a different colour at almost every pH number. It is sold as a liquid or as pH paper.
terms.example: A pH paper strip turns red in lemon juice, green in water and blue in soapy water.
terms.art: A strip of pH paper beside a colour chart that runs from red to violet, with numbers 0 to 14 under it.

terms.meaning: Neither acidic nor basic. A neutral liquid has equal amounts of acid-type and base-type particles.
terms.example: Pure water is neutral, at pH 7.
terms.art: A balance with two equal piles of tiny particles, one marked acid and one marked base.

terms.meaning: A strong acid, called hydrochloric acid, that cells in the stomach wall make on purpose. It starts the digestion of protein and kills many germs that arrive with food.
terms.example: The acid in an empty stomach is about pH 1 to 2, strong enough to sting a cut.
terms.art: A cut-open stomach showing a pool of acid in the middle and a thick layer of slimy mucus along the wall.

terms.meaning: A natural helper made by living cells that speeds up one kind of change, such as breaking food into smaller pieces. Each enzyme works best at its own pH.
terms.example: The enzyme pepsin, in the stomach, breaks the protein in dal, egg and paneer into smaller pieces.
terms.art: A big protein chain being cut into small pieces by a pair of scissors labelled pepsin.

terms.meaning: A thick, slippery, wet coating made by cells. Mucus protects the soft inside of the stomach, the nose and the throat.
terms.example: The mucus in the stomach holds a little base, so the stomach wall stays close to neutral even when the middle of the stomach is full of acid.
terms.art: A thin slice of stomach wall with a coloured layer of mucus between the wall and the acid.

terms.meaning: A burning feeling in the chest that happens when stomach acid splashes up into the food pipe, which has no mucus shield.
terms.example: A very big, oily meal can make acid splash up when you lie down straight after eating.
terms.art: A body outline with a food pipe and a stomach, and a few drops of acid splashing up into the pipe.

terms.meaning: A medicine or powder that is a base. It reacts with stomach acid and uses some of it up.
terms.example: Milk of magnesia, cooking soda and many chewable tablets work as antacids.
terms.art: A white tablet dropping into a pool of acid, with the acid level getting lower.

terms.meaning: To use up acid by adding a base, or use up a base by adding acid, until the mixture moves towards neutral.
terms.example: Cooking soda neutralises vinegar and makes fizzing carbon dioxide gas.
terms.art: A glass of pink liquid turning purple as a scoop of white powder is added.

terms.meaning: A gentle base. Cooking soda is sodium bicarbonate. Your own body also makes bicarbonate to protect the stomach wall and to neutralise acid after the stomach.
terms.example: Fruit salt such as Eno holds bicarbonate and a dry acid. It fizzes in water, because the two meet and react.
terms.art: A packet of cooking soda and a tiny drawing of the stomach wall releasing bubbles of bicarbonate.

terms.meaning: A spiral-shaped bacterium that lives in the stomachs of about half of all people. Most of the time it does no harm. Sometimes it causes sore patches, called ulcers.
terms.example: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed in the 1980s that this bacterium causes most stomach ulcers.
terms.art: A spiral-shaped bacterium drawn big, burrowing into the mucus of a stomach wall.

terms.meaning: A sore patch in the stomach wall or the first part of the small intestine, where the protective layer has worn away.
terms.example: Most ulcers are caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori or by some painkillers.
terms.art: A cut-away of the stomach wall with a small crater-shaped sore in the lining.

explanations.context: Last year you sorted liquids by colour from sour to soapy. This card says what the pH number is really counting.
explanations.definition: pH is a number that tells how many free hydrogen ions a watery liquid holds. The more hydrogen ions, the lower the pH.
explanations.description: Last year you met the idea that acids give out tiny charged particles of hydrogen when they dissolve in water. Those are hydrogen ions, and pH counts them. Even pure water has a very few of them. About one water particle in every 500 million splits in two. It makes one hydrogen ion and one partner particle called a hydroxide ion, always in equal numbers. So pure water is balanced, and its pH is 7. An acid adds hydrogen ions, so the pH falls below 7. A base takes hydrogen ions out of the water or adds hydroxide ions, so the pH rises above 7. Most everyday liquids lie between 0 and 14. Very strong acids go below 0, and very strong bases go above 14.
examples: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2. It holds a great many hydrogen ions.
Pure water has a pH of 7. Its hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions are equal in number.
Soapy water has a pH of about 9 or 10. It holds very few hydrogen ions and many hydroxide ions.
explanations.art: Three zoomed-in glasses: lemon juice with many red dots, water with a few red dots and a few blue dots in equal numbers, and soapy water with mostly blue dots.

explanations.concept: Every step on the pH scale is ten times bigger
explanations.context: The pH scale looks like a ruler from 0 to 14. This card is about why it is not a ruler.
explanations.definition: A drop of one pH number means ten times as many hydrogen ions. A rise of one pH number means ten times fewer.
explanations.description: On a ruler, every step is the same size. The pH scale is different. Each step multiplies by ten. Vinegar at pH 3 has ten times as many hydrogen ions as a drink at pH 4. Lemon juice at pH 2 has ten times as many as vinegar, and a hundred times as many as the drink at pH 4. From lemon juice at pH 2 up to pure water at pH 7 is five steps. That is ten times ten times ten times ten times ten, which is 100,000. So lemon juice has 100,000 times as many hydrogen ions as pure water. Scientists use scales like this when numbers swing very wide. The small numbers on the pH scale hide huge differences. Earthquake magnitudes work in a similar way, because each whole number is about ten times more shaking.
examples: pH 3 holds 100 times as many hydrogen ions as pH 5.
The acid in an empty stomach, at pH 2, holds about 250,000 times as many hydrogen ions as blood, at pH 7.4.
A tiny drop of strong acid in a glass changes the pH of plain water by many steps at once.
explanations.art: A ladder with rungs numbered 2 to 7 and a pile of dots beside each rung, each pile ten times bigger than the one above it.

explanations.concept: Indicators: dyes that show hydrogen ions
explanations.context: You used red cabbage water to sort liquids last year. This card says why a dye can change colour, and what other indicators do.
explanations.definition: An indicator is a dye whose colour changes with the number of hydrogen ions around it.
explanations.description: A dye particle is made of atoms joined in a shape. When hydrogen ions attach to it, or let go of it, the shape changes a little. A different shape soaks up different colours of light, so we see a different colour. Red cabbage holds a dye called anthocyanin. It is red at pH 1 to 3, purple near pH 6 to 7, blue near pH 8 to 9, green near pH 10 to 12, and yellow above that. Litmus, a dye from lichens, is red in acids and blue in bases. Turmeric is yellow in acids and turns red in bases. That is why kumkum, which is made from turmeric and lime, is red. Universal indicator is a mixture of several dyes, so it gives a different colour at almost every number. Cabbage colours are only rough. They change with the cabbage, the water and the light.
examples: Red cabbage water turns pink in vinegar and green in washing powder water.
Turmeric water turns red when a pinch of cooking soda is stirred in.
Butterfly pea flower tea is blue, turns purple in lemon juice and turns green in soapy water.
explanations.art: A dye particle drawn in two shapes with a hydrogen ion attached to one, and two glasses beside them in different colours.

explanations.concept: pH paper and pH meters: how exact is a reading?
explanations.context: A colour can only tell you so much. This card is about how scientists get an exact number.
explanations.definition: A pH strip gives a number by matching its colour to a chart. A pH meter gives a number by measuring a tiny electric voltage.
explanations.description: pH paper is a strip soaked in several indicators. You dip it, wait a few seconds, and match its colour to the chart on the pack. Most strips read whole numbers, so they are good to about one step. A step is ten times, so even that is a very useful reading. A pH meter has a thin glass bulb on a probe. The glass makes a tiny voltage that changes with the number of hydrogen ions on the other side. The meter turns the voltage into a number, and a good one reads to one hundredth of a step. A dark or coloured liquid can hide a strip's colour, and a dirty probe gives a wrong number. So scientists measure again, rinse between samples, and say how sure they are.
examples: A strip dipped in lemon juice turns red-orange and reads about 2.
A school pH meter reads a glass of plain water at 7.1 and a glass of left-open water at 6.4.
Cabbage water can tell pink from purple from green, but it cannot tell pH 4 from pH 5.
explanations.art: A pH strip dipped in a glass beside its colour chart, and a pH meter with a thin glass probe in a second glass.

explanations.concept: Stomach acid: an acid made on purpose
explanations.context: The burning in heartburn comes from stomach acid. This card says what that acid is and why the stomach makes it.
explanations.definition: Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, which cells in the stomach wall make and pour into the stomach.
explanations.description: Cells in the wall of your stomach pump hydrogen ions and chloride ions into the stomach, so it holds hydrochloric acid. On an empty stomach the pH is about 1 to 2. While food is inside, the pH rises for a while, and then the stomach makes more. The acid does three jobs. It kills many germs that arrive on food. It unfolds the long protein chains in dal, egg and paneer, so they can be cut. And it wakes up pepsin, an enzyme that the stomach makes in a sleeping form. Pepsin cuts protein into smaller pieces. The stomach can start making acid before the food even arrives. The sight and smell of a hot sambar are enough.
examples: Pepsin works best at about pH 2. In plain water, it hardly works at all.
People with too little stomach acid get some infections of the gut more easily.
The sight and smell of food can start the stomach making acid, a few minutes before the first bite.
explanations.art: A cut-open stomach with a plate of dal and rice approaching, pump cells in the wall pushing hydrogen ions in, and pepsin scissors cutting a protein chain.

explanations.concept: Why the stomach does not burn itself
explanations.context: The stomach holds an acid that can sting a cut. This card is about how it avoids being burnt.
explanations.definition: The stomach wall is protected by a coat of mucus that holds a base, and by cells that are replaced every few days.
explanations.description: The stomach wall has three defences. First, a thick coat of mucus covers the wall, like a wet gel. Second, the mucus traps bicarbonate, which is a base. The middle of the stomach is at about pH 2, but the layer touching the wall is close to pH 7. The acid is neutralised on its way through the coat. Third, the cells of the wall live only a few days. New cells keep replacing the worn ones. So the stomach is not safe because it is tough. It is safe because it is being made again, all the time. If the coat thins or the cells are damaged, acid reaches them, and a sore patch called an ulcer can form.
examples: Painkillers such as aspirin can thin the mucus, which is why a doctor says to take them after food.
A small crack in the mucus lets acid reach the cells, and an ulcer can start there.
The mucus coat is a layer a few tenths of a millimetre thick, about as thick as a sheet of card.
explanations.art: A slice of stomach wall: acid at the top at pH 2, a mucus layer with bubbles of bicarbonate in the middle, and the wall at the bottom at pH 7.

explanations.context: A tablet stops the burning in minutes. This card says what the tablet does and what it cannot do.
explanations.definition: An antacid is a base. It reacts with acid and uses some of it up, so the pH rises.
explanations.description: At the top of your stomach, a ring of muscle works like a door. It lets food in and keeps acid down. Sometimes it opens when it should not, and a little acid splashes up into the food pipe. The food pipe has no mucus shield, so it burns. That is heartburn. An antacid is a base such as sodium bicarbonate, calcium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide or aluminium hydroxide. It reacts with the acid and makes a salt and water. The carbonates also make carbon dioxide gas, which may bring a burp. Antacids do not stop the stomach making acid. They only use up what is already there, so the relief lasts from less than an hour to a few hours. Heartburn that comes often needs a doctor, because it can hide other problems. Children should not be given medicines without asking a doctor.
examples: Cooking soda in water, milk of magnesia and chewable tablets all work as antacids.
Eno fruit salt holds bicarbonate and a dry acid. In water, it fizzes, and the liquid left is usually a little basic.
Lying down straight after a big meal makes it easier for acid to splash up.
explanations.art: A stomach with its top door slightly open and a few drops of acid rising into the food pipe, and a white tablet dissolving in the acid below.

explanations.concept: The body keeps different places at different pH
explanations.context: Acids and bases are not good or bad in the body. This card is about how the body uses both.
explanations.definition: Different parts of the body are held at different pH, because each part does a job that needs its own pH.
explanations.description: Saliva in your mouth is close to neutral. The stomach is a pool of acid, at pH 1 to 3. Just after the stomach, the pancreas and the gut wall pour out bicarbonate. It neutralises the acid, so the small intestine is near neutral or slightly basic. The enzymes of the intestine work best there. They would stop working in the stomach's acid, and pepsin stops working in the intestine. Your blood is held between pH 7.35 and 7.45. That is a very narrow range, and the lungs, the kidneys and chemicals called buffers all work to keep it there. The skin is a little acidic, at about pH 5, and that keeps many germs down. So the body is not one steady condition. It is a row of rooms, each held at the pH its job needs.
examples: Pepsin is at work in the stomach at pH 2 and stops working in the intestine at about pH 7.
A person whose blood pH falls to 7.0 or rises to 7.8 is seriously ill.
The pancreas releases bicarbonate into the first part of the small intestine. It is the body's own antacid.
explanations.art: A body outline with labelled rooms: mouth near 7, stomach near 2, small intestine near 7 to 8, blood 7.4 and skin near 5, each with a colour.

explanations.concept: A bacterium with an antacid of her own
explanations.context: Doctors once thought no living being could survive stomach acid. This card is about a bacterium that does.
explanations.definition: Helicobacter pylori is a spiral-shaped bacterium that lives in the mucus of the stomach and makes a base to protect herself from the acid.
explanations.description: Helicobacter pylori swims through the mucus until she reaches the layer near the wall, where the pH is close to neutral. On the way, she makes an enzyme called urease. Urease breaks down urea, a chemical that is always present in the stomach, into ammonia. Ammonia is a base. It makes a little cloud of neutral liquid around her. About half of all people carry this bacterium, and most people notice nothing. Sometimes she irritates the wall, and the damage can become an ulcer. Other living beings also thrive in acid. The bacteria that make curd work at pH 4. Some tiny microbes live in volcanic hot springs at a pH close to 0.
examples: The urea breath test finds H. pylori by catching the gas from her urease.
Lactic acid bacteria in curd grow at pH 4, and their own acid slows them down.
Picrophilus, a microbe from hot sulphur springs in Japan, grows at a pH of about 0.7.
explanations.art: A spiral-shaped bacterium inside a layer of mucus with a small bubble of ammonia around her and the acid kept outside.

explanations.concept: Why is human stomach acid so strong?
explanations.context: The stomach acid of humans is strong compared with many other animals. This card gives one idea about why.
explanations.definition: Nobody knows for certain why human stomachs are so acidic. One recent idea is that our ancestors often ate old meat that held many microbes.
explanations.description: In 2015, a group of scientists led by Daniel Beasley compared the stomach acidity of many animals. They found that humans are more acidic than most animals that eat meat. Our stomachs are more like those of scavengers such as vultures, which eat old meat. The scientists suggested that strong acid protects a scavenger from the germs in food that has been lying around. They think our ancestors may have eaten carrion often enough that the acid was worth having. But this is an idea and not a settled fact. Other scientists say the strong acid may also help us get the most from protein, or protect against the huge number of microbes in all food.
examples: A vulture can eat old meat that would make most animals ill.
Humans, vultures and some other scavengers all have very acidic stomachs.
Animals that mostly eat leaves tend to have milder stomach acid.

perspectives.explanation: Strong acid evolved because our ancestors ate carrion, and it cleared out the germs.
The acid may be more about digesting protein and protecting against the many microbes on all food, and not about carrion.

explanations.art: A vulture beside a human at a table, each with a drawing of a very acidic stomach, and a question mark between them.

explanations.concept: Hydrogen ions power every living cell
explanations.context: Hydrogen ions do more than make things sour. This card is about the job they do in all living cells, including yours.
explanations.definition: Living cells keep a difference in hydrogen ions across a thin wall, and use it like a battery.
explanations.description: Inside every cell of your body, tiny parts called mitochondria pump hydrogen ions across a thin wall. There are more hydrogen ions on one side than on the other, like water held behind a dam. The ions can flow back only through a tiny machine in the wall, called ATP synthase. As they pour through, they turn the machine like a mill wheel, and it makes ATP. ATP is the small packet of energy that every cell spends. Peter Mitchell worked out this idea in 1961, and he won the Nobel Prize in 1978. Your stomach cells use a similar pump to make stomach acid. Some scientists think the first living cells may have used a difference in pH at warm vents on the sea floor. That idea is not settled.
examples: Every breath you take feeds a hydrogen ion pump in each of your cells.
The pump in your stomach wall, which makes acid, is the target of some heartburn medicines.
Plants use a hydrogen ion difference in their leaves to turn sunlight into stored energy.
explanations.art: A tiny cell with a mitochondrion, a wall with many red dots on one side, and a small water wheel turning as dots pour through it.

explanations.concept: Acids and bases in soil and in dye vats
explanations.context: pH matters outside the body too. This card is about soil, flowers and the dyer's vat.
explanations.definition: Soil and dye vats each have a pH, and the plants and microbes that live in them do best in a certain range.
explanations.description: Tea plants grow best in acidic soil, at about pH 4.5 to 5.5, and the hills of the Nilgiris and Assam have soil like that. Many vegetables do better in soil closer to pH 6 to 7. A farmer can spread lime on soil that is too acidic, and the lime acts as an antacid for the soil. The hydrangea flowers of Ooty and Kodaikanal are blue in acidic soil and pink in less acidic soil, because soil acidity changes how much aluminium the roots can take up. A traditional indigo dye vat is kept basic, at about pH 10 to 11, and the dye stops working if the vat turns sour. Dyers add lime to keep it right.
examples: Tea in the Nilgiris grows in acidic soil, at about pH 5.
Blue hydrangeas grow where the soil is acidic. Pink ones grow where it is less acidic.
A dyer adds lime to an indigo vat when its pH has fallen.
explanations.art: A tea garden on a hill with a pH ruler stuck into the soil, a blue hydrangea beside a pink one, and an indigo vat with a lime bag next to it.

agreed.text: pH measures the number of free hydrogen ions in a watery liquid, and each step on the scale is a tenfold change.
agreed.evidence: The scale was set out by Søren Sørensen in 1909. Instruments that count hydrogen ions agree with it, and pH meters read it to a hundredth of a step.

agreed.text: Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, with a pH of about 1 to 2 in an empty stomach.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have measured the pH inside living stomachs with a thin probe passed down the food pipe, and the numbers are the same in many studies.

agreed.text: The stomach protects itself with a mucus coat that traps bicarbonate, and with cells that are replaced every few days.
agreed.evidence: Probes that measure pH layer by layer have shown a smooth change, from about pH 2 in the middle of the stomach to about pH 7 at the wall.

agreed.text: Antacids are bases. They use up stomach acid, and the relief lasts only until the stomach makes more.
agreed.evidence: Studies that measure stomach pH after an antacid show the pH rising within minutes and falling back within an hour or two.

agreed.text: Most stomach ulcers are caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori or by some painkillers, and not by stress or spicy food.
agreed.evidence: In 1984 Barry Marshall drank the bacterium and developed gastritis. Large trials later showed that killing the bacterium with antibiotics cured most ulcers for good.

agreed.text: Blood is held in a very narrow range, between pH 7.35 and 7.45, whatever a person eats.
agreed.evidence: Blood tests from large numbers of healthy people show this range. Breathing, the kidneys and chemical buffers keep it steady.

challenging.claim: Stomach ulcers are caused by stress, spicy food and too much acid.
challenging.for: Ulcers do happen more in stressed people, and an ulcer hurts more after spicy food. Acid-blocking medicines did ease the pain.
challenging.against: Marshall and Warren found a bacterium in the stomachs of people with ulcers. Marshall drank the bacterium and got sick. Antibiotics cured ulcers for good, while acid-blockers alone let them return.

challenging.claim: A pH of 3 is only a little more acidic than a pH of 4.
challenging.who: Many people who look at the numbers.
challenging.for: The numbers are next to each other on the scale, and they look close.
challenging.against: Each step on the pH scale is ten times. pH 3 holds ten times as many hydrogen ions as pH 4, and pH 2 holds a hundred times as many.

challenging.claim: Cabbage water tells you the exact pH of a liquid.
challenging.for: The colour does change in a steady way from red through purple to green.
challenging.against: Cabbage colours change with the cabbage, the water and the light, and a colour can only separate pH values that are a few steps apart. A pH meter reads far more exactly.

challenging.claim: It is harmless to take an antacid after every meal.
challenging.for: Antacids are cheap and easy to buy, and an occasional tablet is fine for most adults.
challenging.against: Heartburn that comes often can be a sign of another problem, and a doctor should look at it. Some antacids also cause stomach upset, and strong long-term acid-reducing medicines have risks that doctors are still studying.

challenging.claim: No living being can survive in strong acid.
challenging.who: Doctors before 1982, and many people today.
challenging.for: Strong acid burns skin and kills most bacteria on contact.
challenging.against: Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomach. Curd bacteria grow in acid at pH 4. Some microbes in volcanic hot springs grow at a pH close to 0.

big_questions.q: The stomach holds an acid that can sting a cut, and it never burns itself. Is the stomach a thing that stays the same, or something the body keeps making again?
big_questions.hint: Think about the mucus coat, and about cells that last only a few days.

big_questions.q: pH 2 and pH 5 look close on the scale. Why is it a mistake to think they are close?
big_questions.hint: Think about the dye ladder, where every cup held ten times less colour.

big_questions.q: Stomach acid is bad in the food pipe and good in the stomach. Is anything good or bad on its own, or only in a place?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the same chemical is doing a useful job and where it is doing harm.

big_questions.q: For decades, doctors trusted a belief that no bacterium could live in stomach acid. How do we decide whether to trust an expert or a young doctor with a strange idea?
big_questions.hint: Think about what Marshall did to show he was right, and what evidence a strange idea needs.

big_questions.q: Helicobacter pylori makes a base around herself to survive in acid. Did she decide to do that, or is it only chemistry? What would you need to see to know?
big_questions.hint: Think about how the bacterium swims to the wall, and what she senses on the way.

big_questions.q: Your blood stays at pH 7.4 while your stomach sits at pH 2. What must the body keep doing, every moment, to stay as it is?
big_questions.hint: Think about breathing, the kidneys and the pancreas pouring out bicarbonate.

big_questions.q: The colour in a cabbage leaf changes with acid. Is the colour a measurement, or is it a message for someone? Who might it be for?
big_questions.hint: Think about leaves that turn red in autumn, flowers that call bees and the cabbage's own life.

big_questions.q: Sour means something different to a child, a bee and a bacterium. Do we all taste the same world?
big_questions.hint: Think about what hydrogen ions mean to a tongue, to a bacterium that swims away from them and to a bacterium that grows in them.

big_questions.q: Hydrogen ions power your cells and also burn your food pipe. Can one thing be a gift and a danger at once?
big_questions.hint: Think about the dam and the water wheel, and about water held back behind a thin wall.

story.title: The Vat That Was Sulking
story.note: A made-up story. The village and the people are imagined. The science in it is real. A traditional indigo vat is kept basic, usually at about pH 10 to 11, and it stops working when it turns sour. Dyers differ in how they judge a vat and which ingredients they add with the lime. Avuri is the Tamil name for the indigo plant. Lime water is strongly basic and burns skin, so only a grown-up should handle it.
text: Every summer, Vimala spent two weeks in a village in Tirunelveli district with her great-aunt, Valli Paati. Paati dyed cloth blue. Behind her house stood a low shed, and in the shed sat a clay vat as wide as a bullock-cart wheel, full of dark water that smelled of wet leaves.

The dye came from avuri, the indigo plant. Paati's family had soaked avuri leaves in that vat for as long as anyone remembered, with a little lime to keep the water right. Vimala loved what happened next. Paati dipped a white cotton towel into the dark water and counted to sixty. When she lifted it out, the towel dripped yellow-green, the colour of a lemon leaf. Then, in the open air, it turned blue before Vimala's eyes, a little more with every breath, until it was the blue of the sky just after sunset.
This summer, the magic did not come. Paati dipped a towel, counted to sixty, and lifted it out. It was a pale, streaky grey. She dipped it again, and again. It stayed grey.
Paati bent over the vat and sniffed. She shook her head. 'The vat is sulking,' she said. 'She has gone sour, and I do not know why.'
Her grandson Murali, who was twelve, had come for the day with a sack of lime on his shoulder. 'Easy,' he said. 'Lime fixes everything. Tip in the whole sack.'

'Too little and she sulks,' said Paati. 'Too much and she burns, and the tiny living beings in her stop their work. My mother knew the right amount by the feel of the water and a touch of it on her tongue. I know it by my nose. But my nose is old this year.' She looked at Vimala. 'And you must never taste a vat. Never.'

Vimala thought of the pencil box in her bag. Her Class 4 teacher, Kalpana Miss, had given every child a small roll of pH paper. Vimala unrolled a strip and rinsed a steel cup. 'May I try something, Paati?'

Paati nodded and ladled out a cup of the dark water. Vimala dipped a strip for one second, as Kalpana Miss had taught her. The tip came out stained, but the clean middle of the strip matched the number 8 on the chart.
Then she ran next door, where Selvi Akka's vat worked beautifully, and asked for a cup of her water. The strip matched 10.
'Two steps apart,' said Vimala. 'Every step on the chart is ten times. So Selvi Akka's vat has a hundred times more of the base particles than yours.'
'A hundred times!' said Murali. 'Then I was right. Tip in the sack!'
'No,' said Vimala. 'The chart does not say how much lime a big vat needs. And Paati said too much is wrong as well. We must test it in small cups first.'
Murali opened his mouth, and closed it again.

Vimala set five steel cups on the step, each holding the same ladle of Paati's vat water. Only Paati was allowed to touch the clear lime water. She added it with a spoon: none to the first cup, one spoon to the second, then two, then three, then four. Vimala stirred each cup, dipped a fresh strip, and wrote the number in her notebook. Eight. Nine. Nine. Ten. Eleven.
'Three spoons matches Selvi Akka,' said Vimala. 'Four is past it.'
'But four spoons is stronger,' said Murali. 'So it must be better.'

'Stronger is not better,' said Paati slowly. 'Past the right place, the little ones in her stop. By tomorrow the vat would be as dead as that grey cloth.' She cut a scrap from the towel and dipped it in the first cup. It stayed grey.
'Now try a scrap in the cup with three spoons,' said Vimala. The scrap came out yellow-green. In the air, it turned a deep, clean blue. Even Murali clapped.

A big vat holds hundreds of cups. Paati did not pour in hundreds of spoons at once. She added the lime water in four portions through the day, stirring with her long wooden paddle, and each time Vimala dipped a strip. By evening, the strip matched 10.

The next morning, Paati dipped a white towel, counted to sixty, and lifted it out. It dripped yellow-green. Murali and Vimala held their breath. In the air, it turned blue, and then a deeper blue. 'She is happy,' said Paati. She put the towel in Vimala's hands.
'Your strip told me what my mother's tongue told her,' Paati said. 'And my nose tells me this morning that the vat has stopped sulking. I will keep the nose and the strip both.'
'So lime fixes everything,' said Murali, still thinking.
'Lime fixed this vat, because this vat was too sour,' said Vimala. 'If it had been too strong already, more lime would have hurt it. It is not about more. It is about the right place.'
Murali looked at the roll of strips. 'Can I have one? I want to test the tea.'
Vimala tore him a strip. That evening, she dipped one into the glass of buttermilk Paati gave her. It matched 4. Even a glass of buttermilk, she thought, had its own place on the line.
story.epiphany: The vat did not need more lime. It needed to be in the right place on the pH scale.
ask: Why did Vimala test lime water in small cups before putting any in the big vat?
The strip said the vat was two steps lower than Selvi Akka's. Why did that not mean the vat needed exactly twice as much lime?
If a vat can be too sour and too strong, what does that tell you about the words 'more' and 'better'?
