roots.context: We have measured acids and bases with numbers and raced antacids against a glass of acid. Now we ask what this tells us about the body we live in and the world it is part of.

deep_truth.truth: Your stomach holds a strong acid on purpose, and the pancreas pours out a base right after it. Your blood is kept almost exactly neutral. Acid is not bad and base is not good. A living body holds each place at the pH its job needs.
deep_truth.habit: We call acids harsh and bases gentle, and we hope for a neutral middle. But the body needs strong acid in the stomach and a base just after it. The right place on the scale depends on the job.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Antacid Showdown, each powder moved the same glass of acid along the scale. Too few scoops left it sour, and too many pushed it past purple. The pH Ladder cards show the stomach, the blood and the skin sitting at three different numbers. If your own results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: You are not one steady thing. Your stomach is acid and your blood is nearly neutral, and your body keeps both going every moment.
three.what_is_life: Every living cell uses a difference in hydrogen ions like a battery. Life is held up by differences that are kept, and not by everything being the same.
three.what_is_this_world: Even pure water is a balance of two kinds of particles in equal numbers. Everything sour or soapy is that balance tipped one way or the other.

roots.thread: Pure water is a perfect balance. A very few water particles split into a hydrogen ion and a hydroxide ion, always in equal numbers, so the two cancel exactly. Acid and base are what we get when the balance tips. The stomach tips it one way, the blood holds it level, and the dye vat tips it the other way, all from the same water. In this picture, the one balance shows up as many different places, each with its own job. Nothing is the opposite of anything else. They are two sides of one balance.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that food we eat divides into three. The coarsest part leaves the body, the middle part becomes flesh, and the finest part becomes the mind.
teachings.link: Digestion begins in the acid of the stomach. The acid and the enzymes cut food into pieces small enough to build a body. Dal and rice become you.

teachings.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapter 6
teachings.teaching: Aristotle taught that the right amount is a middle between too much and too little, and that the middle is different for different people. A trained wrestler needs more food than a beginner.
teachings.link: The right pH is also a middle that depends on the place. Pepsin needs pH 2, and blood needs pH 7.4. The same number would be wrong in the other place.

teachings.teaching: All things carry the dark and embrace the light, and by blending their breath they reach harmony.
teachings.link: Acid and base are opposites, and pure water holds them in equal balance. The body uses both to stay in harmony.

science.text: Blood is held between pH 7.35 and 7.45 by the lungs, the kidneys and chemical buffers, even though the stomach beside it sits at pH 1 to 2.
Strong stomach acid may have evolved because our ancestors often ate old meat, as a vulture does. Daniel Beasley and colleagues suggested this in 2015.

other_view.view: The stomach pumps out hydrogen ions and a bacterium makes ammonia because of chemistry. They would say that chemistry alone holds each pH and makes the ammonia, and that words like keep and choose only describe automatic processes.

practice.title: Smell and wait
practice.say: Sit with a banana, a piece of jaggery or a hot idli. Close your eyes and smell it for one slow breath. Do not eat yet. Notice whether your mouth fills with saliva. Your stomach is getting ready too, with acid and pepsin, before the first bite. Breathe out slowly. Then take one slow bite and chew it twenty times.
practice.kid: Smell your food with your eyes shut. Do not eat yet. Does your mouth feel wet? Your stomach is getting ready too. Now take one slow bite.

ask: Is the acid in your stomach part of you, or something you make and keep apart from you?
If pure water holds acid and base in equal balance, what does it mean to call water neutral?
Is a balance one steady place, or the work of always bringing things back?
roots.art: A body outline split into rooms of different colours, with a glass of plain water at the centre holding equal red and blue dots.

games.title: The pH Ladder: where does it belong?
games.context: This is a guessing game about the pH scale. Each card shows a liquid, and you guess which rung of the ladder it sits on.

setup.art: Fifteen paper rungs numbered 0 to 14 laid in a row on a table, with a pile of twenty cards and a few small markers beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the rungs and cards. Lay the rungs in a row from 0 to 14.

setup.art: A child reading the front of a card that says lemon juice, while two others place markers on rungs of the ladder.
setup.caption: 2. The reader shows a card. Everyone puts a marker on the rung they guess.

setup.art: The same card turned over to show its back with the pH range, and a hand moving a marker to score points.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score points for a guess that is on the card's range.

printables.title: 15 ladder rungs, from 0 to 14, to lay in a row on the table
20 two-sided cards: a liquid on the front, and its pH range with a fact on the back

items.f: Toilet cleaner, which holds a strong acid
items.b: 0 to 1. A strong acid that is never touched. Never mix it with bleach, because the mixture makes a poison gas.

items.f: Stomach acid in an empty stomach
items.b: 1 to 2. Hydrochloric acid, made on purpose by cells in the stomach wall.
2 to 3. Citric acid. Lemon juice holds about 100,000 times as many hydrogen ions as pure water.
2 to 3. Acetic acid. Vinegar is a weak acid, so it is safe on food, but it stings in a cut.
2 to 3. The fizz and the acids in the drink make it sour, and sugar hides the taste.
3 to 4. Citric acid and other fruit acids.
4 to 5. A mild acid, which is why tomatoes taste a little sour.
4 to 5. Lactic acid, made by bacteria that turned milk into curd.
4 to 5. Coffee holds several mild acids.
5 to 6. A little acidic, which keeps many germs down.
5 to 6. Rain takes in carbon dioxide from the air, which makes it a little acidic.
6 to 7. Very close to neutral, and a little acidic.

items.f: Saliva, the water in your mouth
items.b: 6 to 7. Close to neutral, so it does not hurt your teeth or tongue.
7 to 8. Close to neutral, and a little basic in many places because it carries minerals from rock.
7 to 8. Held between 7.35 and 7.45 by your lungs, kidneys and chemical buffers.
8 to 9. A little basic, because the sea holds salts from rock.
8 to 9. Sodium bicarbonate, a gentle base that is used as an antacid.
9 to 10. Soap is a base, which is why soap feels slippery.

items.f: Milk of magnesia, a medicine for heartburn
items.b: 10 to 11. A white liquid of magnesium hydroxide, a base that uses up stomach acid.

items.f: The clear water above slaked lime, or lime water
items.b: 12 to 13. A strong base that burns skin. Only a grown-up touches it.

rules: The ladder has 15 rungs, numbered 0 to 14. Lay them in a row on the table with 0 on the left.
Shuffle the cards into a pile with the front side up. One player is the reader.
The reader shows the top card. It names a liquid. Everyone decides which rung it sits on and puts a marker there.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. The back gives a range of two numbers, such as 2 to 3.
A marker on one of the two numbers scores 2 points. A marker one rung away scores 1 point.
After each card, the reader's job passes to the player on the left. Playing alone, you are your own reader and you keep your own score.
The game ends when all 20 cards have been read. The most points wins. The best score alone is 40, so try to beat your last one.

flow.do: Cut out the 15 rungs and the 20 cards. Lay the rungs in a row from 0 to 14. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: This ladder runs from 0 to 14. Seven is the middle. Low numbers are acids, and high numbers are bases.
flow.kid: Lay the rungs from 0 to 14. Shuffle the cards. Low is acid. High is base.
flow.parent: Show the ladder before the first card. Point out that 7 is neutral, with acids to the left and bases to the right.
flow.context: This is the first step of the pH Ladder game. You set up the ladder and the cards.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. The reader shows each front, everyone places a marker, and then the reader shows the back.
flow.say: Read the front. Everyone puts a marker on the rung they think is right. Then we turn the card and check.
flow.kid: Read a card. Put a marker on a rung. Turn the card. Check your guess.

ask.q: What made you pick that rung?
good: It tastes sour, so it must be an acid.
Soap feels slippery, so it is a base.
I remembered it from the cabbage test.

flow.context: In this step you play the first six cards and learn how to guess.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards. Keep a score on paper. After card four, ask the question below.
flow.say: Keep going. Which liquids so far were closest to 7? Which were the farthest away?
flow.kid: Play on. Keep a score. Which liquids are close to 7?

ask.q: Which liquid was the biggest surprise so far, and why?
good: Tap water was a little basic.
A cold drink was as sour as lemon.
Milk was almost neutral.

flow.context: In this step you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last six cards. Add up the points. Say who won, or whether you beat your last score.
flow.say: Last cards. Think about whether it tastes sour, feels slippery or is used for cleaning.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Add up your points.
flow.context: In this step you finish the pile and count the points.

flow.do: Ask your child to find the cards for the stomach and for the blood on the ladder. Ask how far apart they are.
flow.say: Look at the stomach card and the blood card. How many rungs apart are they? Each rung is ten times.
flow.kid: Find the stomach card and the blood card. How many rungs apart?
flow.think: If each rung is ten times, how many times more hydrogen ions are in the stomach than in the blood?
flow.parent: The stomach, at 1 to 2, and the blood, at 7 to 8, are five or six rungs apart. That is 100,000 to 1,000,000 times as many hydrogen ions.
flow.context: This is the last step of the pH Ladder game. You look back at the cards.

experiments.title: Antacid Showdown: which powder beats the acid with the fewest scoops?
experiments.question: Cooking soda, a crushed antacid tablet, eggshell powder and salt: how many scoops of each does it take to turn a glass of pretend stomach acid from pink to purple?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which powder will need the fewest scoops? Will the salt change the colour at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every glass gets the same 2 tablespoons of vinegar and 4 tablespoons of cabbage water, the same size of scoop and the same 20 seconds of stirring. Only the powder is different. Glass A has cooking soda, B has antacid powder, C has eggshell powder and D has salt. Salt is not a base, so glass D is the control. A plain purple glass T is the target to match.

materials.item: 5 clear glasses or small white cups, marked A, B, C, D and T
about 150 millilitres of vinegar (a small cup of it)
red cabbage water: 3 big red cabbage leaves blended with 1 and a half cups of water and strained. No red cabbage? Soak a handful of butterfly pea flowers (sangu poo) in hot water.
a tablespoon and a level quarter-teaspoon measure
cooking soda, one tablespoon of it
4 plain white chewable antacid tablets (from a chemist, bought by a grown-up), crushed to a fine powder between two spoons
eggshell powder: the shells of 2 eggs, washed, dried in the sun and crushed fine. If your family does not eat eggs, use a second kind of white antacid tablet.
a pinch of table salt, 5 teaspoons for stirring, a clock, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Vinegar is mild, but keep it away from eyes. Do not taste anything in the glasses. Antacid tablets are medicine, so a grown-up crushes them and puts the rest back in the packet, out of reach of small children. Wash your hands afterwards and pour everything down the sink.
experiments.record: Write the number of scoops each powder needed and what the colour did after two extra scoops. Then draw a bar for each powder.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make a glass of pretend stomach acid and race four powders against it. You count the scoops each one needs.

setup.art: Four white powders in four small bowls labelled cooking soda, antacid, eggshell and salt, beside five clear glasses marked A, B, C, D and T.
setup.caption: 1. Set out the four powders and five glasses.

setup.art: A hand pouring 2 tablespoons of vinegar and 4 tablespoons of cabbage water into a glass, which turns pink.
setup.caption: 2. Put vinegar and cabbage water in A, B, C and D. They turn pink.

setup.art: A level quarter-teaspoon of white powder being tipped into a pink glass, with small bubbles rising.
setup.caption: 3. Add one level scoop of powder to a glass and stir for 20 seconds.

setup.art: A pink glass next to a purple target glass T, with a child comparing them and writing a number in a table.
setup.caption: 4. Count scoops until the glass matches the purple target.

flow.do: Show your child the four powders in four bowls. Read out their names. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: These are four powders. Cooking soda, crushed antacid tablet, eggshell powder and salt. Which will beat the acid? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Here are four powders. Which one beats the acid? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which powder will need the fewest scoops, and why?
good: The antacid, because it is made for stomach acid.
Cooking soda, because it fizzed with lemon last year.
Not the salt, because it is not a base.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Antacid Showdown. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Make the cabbage water and strain it. Fill glass T with 4 tablespoons of cabbage water and 2 tablespoons of plain water.
flow.say: This purple glass is our target. We want every acid glass to match it. Purple means the acid is used up.
flow.kid: Make the cabbage water. Fill glass T. This purple is the target.
flow.parent: If you use butterfly pea flowers, the target is blue-violet and the acid glasses are pink-purple. Match the target as best you can. Keep the glass T next to the others the whole time.
flow.context: In this step you make the indicator and the target glass. The target is the colour that means the acid is used up.

flow.do: Put 2 tablespoons of vinegar and 4 tablespoons of cabbage water into each of glasses A, B, C and D. Stir.
flow.say: Each glass now holds the same pretend stomach acid. It is pink. Only the powder will be different.
flow.kid: Put vinegar and cabbage water in glasses A to D. Stir. They turn pink.

check.q: Why does every glass get exactly the same vinegar and cabbage water?
options: So that only the powder is different, and any difference comes from the powder
So that the glasses look neat
So that the vinegar lasts longer
check.why: A fair test changes one thing at a time. If the acid were different in each glass, we could not tell whether the powder or the acid made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you build four glasses of pretend stomach acid. They are all the same, so the test is fair.

flow.do: Glass A gets cooking soda, B gets antacid powder, C gets eggshell powder and D gets salt. Add one level scoop to A and stir for 20 seconds. Look at the colour. Add another scoop. Stop when A matches glass T, or after 8 scoops. Do B, C and D the same way.
flow.say: Add one scoop, stir for 20 seconds, and look. Is it still pink? Add another. Keep counting until it matches the target. Write down the number of scoops.
flow.kid: Add one scoop. Stir. Look at the colour. Add another. Count the scoops. Stop at purple.

ask.q: What do you see on the top of glass A after the first scoop?
good: Bubbles.
Fizz.
The colour starts to change.

flow.parent: Eggshell powder reacts slowly, so stir it for a full minute. Antacid powder may stay cloudy, so judge the colour of the liquid. If a glass has not matched after 8 scoops, write 'more than 8'. Salt should do nothing at all.

check.q: Salt is added to glass D and the colour stays pink. What does this show?
options: The colour change in the other glasses comes from the powder being a base, and not just from stirring in a powder
Salt is a stronger acid than vinegar
Salt is the best powder for heartburn
check.why: Glass D is the control. Salt is neither an acid nor a base, so it does nothing to the colour. This shows that the other powders did something special.

flow.context: In this step you add the powders scoop by scoop and count until each glass matches the target.

flow.do: Take the first glass that matched the target. Add two more scoops of the same powder. Look at the colour and write it in the last column.
flow.say: Now we go past the target. Add two more scoops. What colour is it now?
flow.kid: Add two more scoops to the purple glass. What colour is it now?
flow.think: Is a base that is too strong better than one that is just right?
flow.parent: A glass that was purple often turns blue after two more scoops. That means the mixture is now a base, and not an acid. If nothing changes, write that down. Cooking soda and eggshell can only push a glass a little way.
flow.context: In this step you add too much powder on purpose, to see what happens when the base goes past the target.

flow.do: Draw a bar for each powder, showing its scoops. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Pour everything down the sink.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each powder. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: A person takes two tablets for heartburn. Another takes ten. Why might ten be worse than two?
flow.parent: A strong answer names the powder that needed the fewest scoops, says that salt did nothing, and says that extra scoops pushed the colour past purple. After they speak, explain: the powders that worked are bases. A base uses up acid until the mixture is neutral. Past that, more base makes the mixture basic. Scoop counts depend on how fine the powder is, so your numbers may differ from someone else's. That is also a result.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Antacid Showdown. You draw your results and explain what you found.

experiments.title: The Ten-Times Ladder: how far can a colour be made weaker?
experiments.question: If you make a colour ten times weaker, again and again, after how many steps can you no longer see it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After how many cups will the colour be gone? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every cup gets exactly 9 teaspoons of plain water and exactly 1 teaspoon from the cup before. The spoon is rinsed between cups, and the same white paper stands behind every cup. Only the number of steps changes.
results_table: Parts of dye water in the cup
Colour you can see (5 is dark, 0 is none)

materials.item: 7 small clear cups or glasses, numbered 0 to 6
a small bottle of dark food colour (red or blue works well), or half a cup of very strong tea
a teaspoon, a jug with 1 litre of plain water and a cup for rinsing the spoon
a sheet of white paper, a marker and the results table

experiments.safety: Food colour stains clothes and hands, so wear an old shirt and wipe up drips. Do not drink anything in the cups.
experiments.record: Write a number from 5 to 0 for the colour in each cup. Then write the cup number where the colour was last easy to see, and work out how many times weaker it is than cup 0.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make a colour ten times weaker again and again. It shows what a ten-times step on the pH scale feels like.

setup.art: A row of seven clear cups numbered 0 to 6 on a table, with a bottle of dark food colour and a jug of water beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Set out seven cups numbered 0 to 6.

setup.art: A teaspoon moving water into cup 0, with three drops of dark colour falling in.
setup.caption: 2. Make cup 0: ten teaspoons of water and three drops of colour.

setup.art: A teaspoon carrying a little coloured water from cup 0 into cup 1, which already holds nine teaspoons of plain water.
setup.caption: 3. Move one teaspoon from cup 0 into cup 1, and stir.

setup.art: A row of seven cups with colours fading from dark red to nearly clear, and a sheet of white paper behind them.
setup.caption: 4. Carry on to cup 6. Look at the row against white paper.

flow.do: Show your child the seven cups in a row. Explain that each cup will hold ten times less colour than the one before. Write down their guess and reason.
flow.say: We will make a colour ten times weaker, again and again. In which cup will you stop seeing it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each cup gets ten times less colour. In which cup will you stop seeing it? Why?

ask.q: In which cup do you think the colour will disappear, and why?
good: Cup 3, because 3 steps is a lot.
Cup 6, because ten times weaker still leaves something.
Cup 2, because it will go quickly.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write it above the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ten-Times Ladder. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Put 10 teaspoons of water into cup 0 and add 3 drops of food colour. Stir. Put 9 teaspoons of plain water into each of cups 1 to 6.
flow.say: Cup 0 gets the colour. Cups 1 to 6 get nine teaspoons of plain water each. Count each spoon with me.
flow.kid: Cup 0 gets colour. Put nine spoons of plain water in cups 1 to 6.
flow.parent: Count the spoons out loud. Use level teaspoons and keep the number the same each time. If you have no teaspoon, use a small medicine cap and keep that size for every step.
flow.context: In this step you make the strongest cup and fill the other cups with plain water.

flow.do: Take 1 teaspoon from cup 0 and stir it into cup 1. Rinse the spoon. Take 1 teaspoon from cup 1 and stir it into cup 2. Carry on to cup 6.
flow.say: One spoon from cup 0 goes into cup 1. Stir. Rinse. One spoon from cup 1 goes into cup 2. Keep going to cup 6.
flow.kid: Move one spoon from cup 0 to cup 1. Stir. Rinse. Carry on to cup 6.

check.q: Cup 1 holds 1 teaspoon of colour water and 9 teaspoons of plain water. How does cup 1 compare with cup 0?
options: Its colour is 10 times weaker
Its colour is 9 times weaker
Its colour is 2 times weaker
check.why: One spoon of coloured water is mixed into ten spoons in all, so the colour is spread over ten times as much water. The colour is ten times weaker.

flow.context: In this step you make the ladder by moving one spoon from each cup to the next.

flow.do: Hold white paper behind the row. Give each cup a number from 5 to 0 for its colour. Mark the last cup where you can still see colour.
flow.say: Look at the cups against the white paper. Give each one a number. Five is dark. Zero is no colour. Where do you stop seeing it?
flow.kid: Look at the row. Give each cup a number from 5 to 0. Where does the colour stop?

ask.q: What do you notice about how the colour changes from cup to cup?
good: It gets paler each time.
The first steps change the most.
Cup 6 looks like plain water.

check.q: Cup 5 looks like plain water. Is the dye gone?
options: No. It is only too little to see, about 1 part in 100,000
Yes. It has vanished
Yes. It has turned into water
check.why: Nothing is ever lost when you dilute. The dye is still there, spread through the water. We just cannot see so little of it. Weak things can be present without being seen.

flow.context: In this step you look at the cups and rate how dark each colour is.

flow.do: Count the steps from cup 0 to the last cup where you saw colour. Work out how many times weaker that cup is than cup 0. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Count the steps to the last cup you can see. How many times weaker is it?
flow.think: Lemon juice is pH 2 and pure water is pH 7. How many cups of this ladder would that be?
flow.parent: If the colour was last visible in cup 4, that is 4 steps, so 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 10,000 times weaker. After they speak, explain: pH works like this. Each step is ten times. Lemon juice to water is 5 steps, so 100,000 times. The dye is a stand-in for hydrogen ions. Your cups may fade sooner or later, depending on the dye. That is also a result.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Ten-Times Ladder. You count the steps and link them to the pH scale.

activities.title: The Eno Mystery: is fruit salt an acid or a base?

materials.item: 1 level teaspoon of plain fruit salt such as Eno (the unflavoured kind)
half a cup of red cabbage water, and 3 teaspoons of vinegar
2 clear glasses, a teaspoon and a glass of plain cabbage water to compare

activities.safety: Do not drink the mixture, because it is a test. Wash your hands afterwards.
activities.record: Write the colour of the cabbage water before, after the fizz, and after each teaspoon of vinegar.
activities.context: In this activity, you test fruit salt, a common antacid, with cabbage water. Fruit salt has an acid and a base in the same packet.

setup.art: A spoonful of white fruit salt held above a glass of purple cabbage water, with a packet beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Pour half a cup of cabbage water into a glass.

setup.art: The fruit salt fizzing in the glass of cabbage water, with a second glass of plain cabbage water beside it for comparison.
setup.caption: 2. Stir in the fruit salt and watch the fizz.

setup.art: A teaspoon of vinegar being added to the glass, which changes colour towards pink.
setup.caption: 3. Add vinegar a teaspoon at a time and watch the colour.

flow.do: Show your child the fruit salt and the glass of cabbage water. Write down their guess and reason.
flow.say: This is fruit salt. It fizzes in water, and people drink it for heartburn. Is it an acid or a base? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Is fruit salt an acid or a base? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Do you think fruit salt is an acid or a base, and why?
good: A base, because it helps heartburn.
An acid, because it fizzes like lemon and soda.
Both, because it fizzes.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Keep the plain cabbage water glass next to the test glass for comparison.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Eno Mystery. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pour half a cup of cabbage water into a glass. Stir in a level teaspoon of fruit salt. Wait until the fizz stops.
flow.say: Watch the fizz. Where do you think the bubbles come from? When it stops, what colour is the water?
flow.kid: Stir in the fruit salt. Watch the fizz. What colour is it when the fizz stops?

ask.q: What colour is the water now, compared with the plain cabbage water?
good: Bluer.
The same purple.
A little pinker.

flow.parent: Eno holds sodium bicarbonate, a dry acid such as citric acid, and sodium carbonate. In water, the acid and bicarbonate meet and fizz with carbon dioxide. The liquid left is usually a little basic, so expect blue or blue-violet. Write down what you actually see.
flow.context: In this step you drop fruit salt into cabbage water and watch the colour.

flow.do: Add one teaspoon of vinegar to the glass and stir. Look at the colour. Add another teaspoon, and another. Write down each colour.
flow.say: Now add vinegar, one teaspoon at a time. What happens to the colour? What does it tell you?
flow.kid: Add vinegar one spoon at a time. What happens to the colour?

check.q: The glass was blue after the fizz and turned purple with vinegar. What does this show?
options: Some base was left over after the fizz, and the vinegar used it up
The vinegar made more bubbles of base
The fruit salt is an acid
check.why: Vinegar is an acid. If it moves the colour back towards purple, there was a base left to use up. That matches an antacid, which has a base ready to neutralise acid.

flow.context: In this step you add vinegar to find out whether the fruit salt left a base behind.

flow.do: Ask your child why the dry powder did not fizz in the packet. Then ask what the water did.
flow.say: In the packet, the acid and the base are both dry and just sit there. Why do they fizz in water? What do you think the water does?
flow.kid: Why does the powder fizz in water and not in the packet?
flow.think: How does an antacid tablet know when to start working?
flow.parent: A good answer says that water lets the acid and the base particles move and meet. Without water, they stay apart. In the stomach, the tablet's base meets the acid in the same way.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Eno Mystery. You think about why water makes the powder fizz.

activities.title: The pH Strip Survey: what are the real numbers?

materials.item: a roll or box of pH paper that reads from 1 to 14, with its colour chart
8 clear cups with 2 tablespoons of each liquid: lemon juice, vinegar, buttermilk, tomato juice, milk, tap water, cooking soda water (a quarter teaspoon in a cup of water) and soapy water
a pencil, a sheet of paper for the table, and a kitchen towel to wipe the strips

activities.safety: Do not taste any of the liquids. Do not touch the soapy water to your eyes. Wash your hands afterwards.
activities.record: Write each liquid and the number from the strip. Then write the liquids in order, from the most acidic to the most basic.
activities.context: In this activity, you use pH paper to find the real numbers for common kitchen liquids. You compare them with your guess.

setup.art: Eight cups of different liquids in a row, each with a paper label, and a roll of pH paper beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put each liquid in its own cup and label it.

setup.art: A pH strip being dipped for one second in a cup of lemon juice and turning orange-red.
setup.caption: 2. Dip a strip for one second.

setup.art: The wet strip held next to the colour chart, with a child writing the matching number.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the strip next to the chart and write the number.

flow.do: Show your child the eight cups. Ask them to put the cups in a row from the most acidic to the most basic. Write down the order.
flow.say: Put these eight liquids in a line from the most sour to the most soapy. Tell me why you chose that order.
flow.kid: Put the cups in a row from sour to soapy. Why that order?

ask.q: Which liquid do you think is the most acidic, and why?
good: Lemon juice, because it is the sourest.
Vinegar, because it stings.
Tomato juice, because it is red and sharp.

flow.parent: Do not correct the order. Write it down so that you can compare it with the numbers later.
flow.context: This is the first step of the pH Strip Survey. You guess an order before you test.

flow.do: Dip a fresh strip into each cup for one second. Hold it next to the chart in daylight. Write the number. Use a new strip for each liquid.
flow.say: Dip a strip for one second. Hold it next to the chart. Which colour does it match? Write down the number.
flow.kid: Dip a strip. Match the colour to the chart. Write the number.

ask.q: Which liquid gave the lowest number, and which gave the highest?
good: Lemon juice was lowest.
Soapy water was highest.
Tap water was close to 7.

flow.parent: Strips differ from one maker to another, so read the chart on your own pack. Read within 30 seconds, or the colour keeps changing. A coloured liquid such as tomato juice may stain the strip. Read the clean middle. If two numbers look equally close, write both.

check.q: Vinegar reads 3 and tomato juice reads 4. Which has more hydrogen ions?
options: Vinegar, about 10 times as many
Tomato juice, about 10 times as many
They have the same number
check.why: A lower pH means more hydrogen ions, and each step is ten times. So vinegar, at pH 3, has about ten times as many as tomato juice, at pH 4.

flow.context: In this step you test each liquid with a pH strip and write the number.

flow.do: Write the liquids in order of their numbers. Compare with your first guess. Circle the biggest surprise.
flow.say: Here is the real order. How close was your guess? Which liquid surprised you most?
flow.kid: Write the real order. Compare it with your guess. Circle the surprise.

ask.q: What surprised you most about the real numbers?
good: Tap water was not exactly 7.
Milk was almost neutral.
Buttermilk was more acidic than I thought.

flow.context: In this step you put the liquids in order of their real numbers.

flow.do: Ask your child to point to where the stomach acid (pH 1 to 2) and the blood (pH 7.4) would go on the table. Ask how many steps apart they are.
flow.say: Stomach acid is about pH 2. Blood is about pH 7.4. Where would they go in our table? How many steps apart are they?
flow.kid: Where would stomach acid go in your table? And blood?
flow.think: If each step is ten times, how many times more acidic is the stomach than the blood?
flow.parent: Stomach acid is more acidic than lemon juice, and blood is just above plain water. They are about five steps apart, which is more than 100,000 times.
flow.context: This is the last step of the pH Strip Survey. You place the stomach and the blood in your table.

activities.title: The Label Hunt: find the base

materials.item: packaging with ingredient lists: an antacid packet, a cooking soda tub, a sachet of fruit salt, a toothpaste tube, a bar of soap or a shampoo bottle, a packet of tamarind or a fruit drink, and a packet of curd or butter
a sheet of paper split into three columns: Acid, Base, Not sure
a pencil

activities.safety: Only read the labels. Do not open cleaners or medicines. Never mix household cleaners. A grown-up handles cleaning products, because some mixtures make poisonous gas.
activities.record: Write each ingredient you find in the column where it belongs, and circle the clue word that told you.
activities.context: In this activity, you read the labels on things at home and spot which ingredients are acids and which are bases.

setup.art: A table with an antacid packet, a toothpaste tube, a soap bar, a cooking soda tub and a tamarind packet laid out in a row.
setup.caption: 1. Gather six or seven things with ingredient lists.

setup.art: A child reading the small print on an antacid packet with a pencil, circling the word hydroxide.
setup.caption: 2. Read the ingredients and circle the clue words.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three columns marked Acid, Base and Not sure, filled in with ingredient names.
setup.caption: 3. Write each ingredient in the right column.

flow.do: Write these clue words on the paper. Words ending in 'acid' are acids. Words with 'hydroxide', 'carbonate' or 'bicarbonate' are bases.
flow.say: Here are the clue words. If the name says acid, it is an acid. If it says hydroxide, carbonate or bicarbonate, it is a base.
flow.kid: Acid in the name means acid. Hydroxide, carbonate or bicarbonate means base.
flow.parent: Examples of acids on labels are citric acid, acetic acid, lactic acid, ascorbic acid and phosphoric acid. Examples of bases are magnesium hydroxide, calcium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate. Magnesium oxide is also a base.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Label Hunt. You learn the clue words.

flow.do: Read the label on each product. Find ingredients with a clue word. Write them in the Acid or Base column. Write other ones under Not sure.
flow.say: Read the ingredients on each product. Do you find a clue word? Which column does it go in?
flow.kid: Read each label. Look for clue words. Write them in a column.

ask.q: Which product had the most clue words, and what were they?
good: The antacid packet had hydroxide and carbonate.
The fruit drink had citric acid.
The toothpaste had a carbonate.

flow.parent: Many toothpastes hold calcium carbonate or sodium bicarbonate. Many fruit drinks and packaged foods hold citric acid. Do not worry about long, hard names. Write them under Not sure.
flow.context: In this step you read labels and look for clue words.

flow.do: Count the acids and the bases. Ask your child which column has the antacid's ingredients.
flow.say: Count the acids and the bases. Which column holds the ingredients of the antacid? Why does that make sense?
flow.kid: Count the acids and the bases. Where is the antacid?

check.q: A label lists 'magnesium hydroxide' as the main ingredient of a heartburn medicine. Why does that make sense?
options: It is a base, so it uses up stomach acid
It is an acid, so it adds to stomach acid
It is a dye that colours the tablet
check.why: An antacid must be a base to use up acid. 'Hydroxide' is the clue word for a base.

flow.context: In this step you count and sort the ingredients.

flow.do: Ask your child why a toothpaste might hold a base.
flow.say: Why do you think a toothpaste holds a base? Think about what the bacteria on your teeth make.
flow.kid: Why might toothpaste hold a base?
flow.think: If bacteria make acid and toothpaste is a base, what does brushing do twice over?
flow.parent: Bacteria on teeth make acid from sugar. A base in toothpaste helps neutralise it. Brushing also removes the bacteria and the leftovers they eat.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Label Hunt. You link toothpaste to what you have learned.

projects.title: The Water Diary: how does the pH of water change?

materials.item: pH paper that reads from 1 to 14, with its colour chart

6 clear cups with 3 tablespoons each of: tap water, filtered or RO water, bottled drinking water, fresh coconut water, water from a potted plant's soil (a tablespoon of soil stirred into 4 tablespoons of water and left to settle for an hour), and rainwater if it has rained
labels, a pencil, a sheet of paper for the table, and a shallow dish to catch rain on a balcony or window ledge

projects.safety: Do not drink any sample, except fresh coconut water if it is clean. Wash your hands after touching soil.

schedule.what: Collect the samples, test them with pH paper, and leave the tap and filtered water uncovered overnight.
Test the tap and filtered water again, compare with yesterday, and write what you notice.

projects.record: Write the pH of each sample on day 1, and again for the tap and filtered water on day 2. Draw a bar for each sample.
projects.context: In this project, you test the pH of water from different places over two days. You find out which samples are acid, neutral or basic.

setup.art: Six labelled cups on a tray: tap water, filtered water, bottled water, coconut water, soil water and rainwater.
setup.caption: 1. Collect six samples in labelled cups.

setup.art: A pH strip being dipped into a cup and held beside a colour chart.
setup.caption: 2. Test each sample with a pH strip.

setup.art: The tap water and filtered water cups left open on a window ledge overnight.
setup.caption: 3. Leave two cups uncovered overnight, and test them again.

flow.do: Fill the cups with the samples and label them. Ask your child to guess the pH of each and to give a reason. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Here are six kinds of water. Which will be the most acidic, and which the most basic? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the pH of each water. Which is the most acid? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which water do you think will be the most acidic, and why?
good: Coconut water, because it tastes slightly sour.
Rainwater, because it comes from the sky.
Soil water, because soil is dirty.

flow.parent: For the soil water, stir a tablespoon of soil into 4 tablespoons of water and let it settle. Test the clear water on top. If it has not rained, skip the rainwater, and write that.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Diary. You collect the samples and guess before you test.

flow.do: Dip a fresh strip in each sample for one second. Match it to the chart and write down the number. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Dip a fresh strip in each cup. Match the colour to the chart. Write down the number for each water.
flow.kid: Dip a strip in each cup. Match the colour. Write the number.

ask.q: Which sample was closest to 7, and which was farthest?
good: Bottled water was nearest to 7.
Coconut water was the most acidic.
Soil water was a little basic.

flow.parent: Tap water in many Indian cities is between 7 and 8.5. Coconut water is a little acidic, near pH 5. Rainwater can be near 5.6 in clean air, but dust can make it nearly neutral. Write what you see, not what you expect.
flow.context: In this step you test each sample with pH paper and write the numbers.

flow.do: Leave the tap water and the filtered water uncovered on a window ledge overnight. Ask your child to guess how their pH will change.
flow.say: We will leave two cups open overnight. Air has carbon dioxide in it. Do you think the pH will go up, go down, or stay the same? Why?
flow.kid: Leave two cups open overnight. Will the pH change? Why?
flow.parent: Carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in water and makes it very slightly more acidic. The change is small, and a strip may not show it. Both results are real.
flow.context: In this step you leave two cups open overnight to see whether the air changes their pH.

flow.wait: Leave the two cups open overnight
flow.do: Test the tap water and the filtered water again with fresh strips. Write down the numbers next to yesterday's numbers.
flow.say: Test the cups again with fresh strips. Is the number the same as yesterday? What changed?
flow.kid: Test the two cups again. Is the number the same?

ask.q: Did the pH of the open cups change, and why do you think so?
good: It went down, because the air put carbon dioxide in.
It stayed the same, because the change was too small.
It went up, because the dust was basic.

check.q: The open water's pH changed from 7 to 6. How much more acidic is it?
options: 10 times as many hydrogen ions
1 time more hydrogen ions
6 times as many hydrogen ions
check.why: One whole step on the pH scale is ten times as many hydrogen ions. So a small-looking drop from 7 to 6 means ten times more hydrogen ions.

flow.context: In this step you test the open cups again and compare with day 1.

flow.do: Draw a bar for each sample. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Pour everything down the sink.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each water. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: Why might a tea garden need acidic soil, while a vegetable bed does not?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Water Diary. You draw your results and explain them.

challenges.title: Shield the Shell: design a coat that keeps acid out
challenges.problem: The stomach wall lives for years in an acid that can sting a cut. Design a coat that keeps vinegar off a piece of eggshell for ten minutes, using only things you find at home. The shell fizzes when vinegar reaches it, so you can see whether your coat works.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
The coat must be thinner than a quarter of a centimetre.
Every piece of shell must be the same size and sit in the same amount of vinegar.
A grown-up does any melting of wax.
You must test your design and count the bubbles.
materials: pieces of clean eggshell about the size of a one-rupee coin (or a seashell, or a plain white antacid tablet with a grown-up)
petroleum jelly, cooking oil, flour paste, a candle for wax, aloe gel, or the slime from a cut okra or soaked isabgol
general: Smear a thick layer of petroleum jelly on a piece of shell, so the vinegar cannot touch it.
Dip a shell in cooled, melted candle wax and let it set (a grown-up does this).
Coat a shell with a thick flour paste and let it dry.
creative: Mix a pinch of cooking soda into aloe gel or okra slime, and coat a shell with it. Now the coat is wet and slimy and holds a base, just like the stomach's mucus.
Add two layers: first a thin layer of gel with soda, and then a thin layer of oil on top.
Try a thick gel without soda next to a thick gel with soda, to find out whether the base makes a difference.
challenges.your_turn: Test three coats and one bare shell in vinegar. Count how long it takes before the first bubble appears and how many bubbles you see after ten minutes. Pick the best coat, and say why you think it worked.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about how the stomach protects itself. You make a coat that keeps acid off a shell, and test it in vinegar.

setup.art: Four pieces of eggshell on a tray: one bare, one with a smear of petroleum jelly, one with a layer of clear gel, and one with gel and a pinch of soda.
setup.caption: 1. Prepare four pieces of shell: one bare and three with different coats.

setup.art: Four small cups of vinegar with one shell placed in each, and a clock beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Put each shell into its own cup of vinegar and start the clock.

setup.art: A child looking at the shells in vinegar, counting the bubbles that appear on each.
setup.caption: 3. Watch for the first bubble and count the bubbles after ten minutes.

flow.do: Wash and dry four pieces of eggshell of the same size. Ask your child to guess which coat will work best, and why.
flow.say: The stomach wall is coated so acid cannot reach it. Which coat do you think will keep the vinegar off best? Why?
flow.kid: Which coat keeps the acid off best? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which coat will work best, and why do you think so?
good: The petroleum jelly, because water cannot get through it.
The gel with soda, because it uses up the acid.
The wax, because it is hard.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Remember that real stomach mucus is a wet gel that holds a base. It does not work like oil.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Shield the Shell challenge. You guess which coat will work.

flow.do: Coat three shells in three different ways. Leave one shell bare. Let the coats set for a few minutes. A grown-up does any melting of wax.
flow.say: Coat three shells in three different ways. Leave one bare. This bare one is our control.
flow.kid: Coat three shells in different ways. Leave one bare.
flow.parent: Wax is hot when melted. A grown-up dips the shell and lets it cool. For the gel with soda, mix one pinch of soda into a spoonful of gel. Keep every coat thin.
flow.context: In this step you make the coats and keep one shell bare as the control.

flow.do: Put 4 tablespoons of vinegar into each of four cups. Drop one shell in each cup and start the clock. Write down when the first bubble appears. After ten minutes, count the bubbles.
flow.say: Drop one shell in each cup and start the clock. Watch for the first bubble. Which shell fizzes first?
flow.kid: Drop a shell in each cup of vinegar. Start the clock. Watch for bubbles.

ask.q: Which shell fizzed first, and which fizzed last or not at all?
good: The bare shell fizzed first.
The petroleum jelly shell did not fizz.
The gel with soda fizzed for a while, then stopped.

flow.parent: The bare shell should fizz at once. A thin gel may let the vinegar through in a minute or two. The gel with soda may fizz on its surface, and that is the coat using up the acid. Write what you see.

check.q: The bare shell fizzes at once. Why is it the control?
options: It shows what happens with no coat, so we can compare the coats with it
It is the best coat
It is the cheapest coat
check.why: A control is the test with nothing changed. It shows the starting result, so we can tell how much each coat helped.

flow.context: In this step you drop each shell in vinegar and watch which coat protects best.

flow.do: Rank the coats from best to worst. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Pour the vinegar down the sink.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Rank the coats. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: The real stomach wall is wet and slimy and holds a base. Which of your coats was most like it?
flow.parent: A strong answer says which coat worked and explains why. An oily coat keeps the acid out by being a barrier. A gel with a base uses up the acid as it comes in, as the real mucus does. After they speak, explain: the stomach uses a thick gel with bicarbonate and replaces its cells every few days. Every coat that wears off is a lesson. If the results were unexpected, say so.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Shield the Shell challenge. You rank the coats and explain what you found.

items.p: Which pH number means a liquid is neutral?
items.why: Seven is the middle of the scale, where acid-type and base-type particles are equal in number. Pure water sits at 7. Zero is a very strong acid, and 14 is a very strong base.

items.p: A liquid with a pH of 2 is an acid.
items.why: True. Any pH below 7 means an acid, and 2 is a strong one. Lemon juice has a pH of about 2.

items.p: Pure water has a pH of ____.
a: seven
items.why: Pure water is neutral. It holds equal numbers of hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions, and its pH is 7.

items.p: Sort each liquid by whether it is an acid, neutral or a base.
items.a: as given
items.why: Lemon juice and vinegar are below 7, so they are acids. Soapy water, cooking soda water and milk of magnesia are above 7, so they are bases. Pure water is at 7.

items.p: On the pH scale, each step down means:
opts: ten times as many hydrogen ions
one more hydrogen ion
the same number of hydrogen ions but a sourer taste
items.why: The pH scale goes up and down in tenfold steps. A drop of one number means ten times as many hydrogen ions. Counting one more ion would be a step on a ruler, and the pH scale is not a ruler.

items.p: Vinegar has a pH of 3 and a drink has a pH of 5. How many times as many hydrogen ions does the vinegar have?
items.why: From pH 5 down to pH 3 is two steps. Each step is ten times, so 10 times 10 is 100. The vinegar has 100 times as many hydrogen ions.

items.p: Where does stomach acid come from?
opts: Cells in the stomach wall make it on purpose
The food that you swallow brings it in
Bacteria from curd make the acid
items.why: Cells in the stomach wall pump hydrogen ions and chloride ions into the stomach. The acid is made by your body for a job. The food does not bring it.

items.p: Match each place in the body to its usual pH.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part of the body is held at the pH its job needs. The stomach is strongly acidic, the skin is a little acidic, saliva is nearly neutral and blood is held in a very narrow range.

items.p: What does an antacid do?
opts: It uses up some of the acid with a base
It stops the stomach making acid for a day
It adds acid to wash the food pipe
items.why: An antacid is a base. It reacts with the acid already in the stomach and uses it up. It does not stop the stomach making more, which is why the relief wears off.

items.p: Heartburn happens in the heart.
items.why: False. Heartburn happens in the food pipe, when stomach acid splashes up and burns it. The name comes from where it feels, in the chest near the heart.

items.p: Cooking soda is also called sodium ____.
a: bicarbonate
items.why: Cooking soda is sodium bicarbonate, a gentle base. It fizzes with vinegar and uses up acid.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Vinegar, lemon juice, milk of magnesia, tomato juice.
items.a: Milk of magnesia, because it is a base. The other three are acids.
items.why: Vinegar, lemon juice and tomato juice are all below pH 7. Milk of magnesia is a base, at about pH 10 to 11, and it is used to treat heartburn.

items.p: In a test of antacids, one glass gets salt, which is not a base. Explain why a test like this needs that glass.
items.a: The salt glass is the control. Salt is not a base, so it should do nothing. If the salt glass stayed pink, then the colour change in the other glasses came from the powders being bases and not from just stirring something in.
items.why: A strong answer says that the control shows what happens when nothing special is added, so we can tell that the other powders did something.

items.p: A friend says a pH of 2 is only a little more acidic than a pH of 3. What would you tell your friend?
items.a: Each step on the pH scale is ten times. A pH of 2 has ten times as many hydrogen ions as a pH of 3. It only looks like a small step because the scale hides the multiplying.
items.why: A strong answer says that each step is ten times and gives the number. The dye ladder showed how quickly ten times adds up.

items.p: Draw a slice of the stomach wall with its three defences: the acid in the middle, a coat of mucus and the wall with new cells.
items.a: A drawing with acid at the top, a thick layer of mucus in the middle with bubbles of bicarbonate, and a wall of cells at the bottom, some of them marked new.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the mucus between the acid and the wall, and says that the mucus holds bicarbonate, a base.

items.p: Put these steps in the right order for how heartburn happens and fades.
a: A big meal fills the stomach
The ring of muscle at the top of the stomach opens when it should not
Acid splashes up into the food pipe
The food pipe has no mucus shield, so it burns
An antacid uses up some of the acid and the burning fades
items.why: The acid must splash up before it can burn. The antacid comes last, because it works on acid that is already there.

worksheets.title: Ten times, mucus and the bacterium (stretch)

items.p: One drink reads pH 4 and another reads pH 6. Which statement is right?
opts: The pH 4 drink has 100 times as many hydrogen ions
The pH 6 drink has 100 times as many hydrogen ions
They differ by only 2 hydrogen ions
items.why: A lower pH means more hydrogen ions, and two steps down is ten times ten, which is 100. The numbers differ by 2, but the amounts differ by 100 times.

items.p: Why does pepsin stop working in the small intestine?
opts: The pH there is near neutral, and pepsin works best in strong acid
The small intestine has no protein
Pepsin is washed away by water
items.why: Each enzyme works best at its own pH. Pepsin likes pH 2, and it stops near pH 7. That is why the body neutralises the acid with bicarbonate after the stomach, so that the intestine's own enzymes can work.

items.p: Past the target colour, adding more antacid powder makes the mixture more acidic.
items.why: False. Once the acid is used up, extra base makes the mixture basic. In the Antacid Showdown, the extra scoops pushed the colour past purple towards blue.

items.p: Match each part of the stomach's defence to what it does.
pairs: Keeps acid from touching the wall
Uses up acid that creeps through
Mends the wall all the time
A ring of muscle at the top
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The stomach has several defences. The mucus is a barrier, the bicarbonate neutralises acid, the new cells mend the wall, and the muscle keeps acid in the stomach.

items.p: Each step on the pH scale is ____ times.
a: ten
items.why: The pH scale goes up and down in tenfold steps, which is why small changes in the number mean large changes in the acid.

items.p: A drink at pH 2 and water at pH 6. How many times as many hydrogen ions does the drink have?
items.why: From pH 6 down to pH 2 is four steps. 10 times 10 times 10 times 10 is 10,000. The drink has 10,000 times as many.

items.p: Here are the results of a girl in Kochi who ran an antacid test. Which powder did not use up the acid, and how can you tell?

chart.title: Scoops used (made-up results; 8 was the limit)

opts: Salt, because it reached the limit of 8 scoops without matching the target
Cooking soda, because it needed the fewest scoops
Eggshell, because it needed the same as cooking soda
items.why: A powder that reaches the limit without matching the target did not use up the acid. Salt is not a base, so this is what we expect. The other powders matched in 3 or 4 scoops.

items.p: Sort each place by how acidic it usually is.
items.a: as given
items.why: The stomach is the strong acid room. Blood and saliva sit near neutral. Skin and tea soil are a little acidic, at about pH 5.

items.p: Put these in order, from the most hydrogen ions to the fewest.
a: lemon juice, pH 2
vinegar, pH 3
buttermilk, pH 4
pure water, pH 7
soapy water, pH 9
items.why: The lower the pH, the more hydrogen ions. Soapy water has the fewest, because it is a base.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Mucus coat, bicarbonate, pepsin, new cells.
items.a: Pepsin, because it digests protein. The other three protect the stomach wall.
items.why: Pepsin is an enzyme that cuts protein in the food. The mucus, the bicarbonate and the new cells all protect the wall from the acid and from pepsin.

items.p: A shop sells 'alkaline water' and says it will make your blood basic. What would you ask, using what you know about blood?
items.a: Blood is held at pH 7.35 to 7.45 by the lungs, the kidneys and chemical buffers, whatever a person eats or drinks. If the pH of blood really changed, a person would be very ill. I would ask what test shows that the water changes blood, and who ran it.
items.why: A strong answer says that blood is held in a narrow range and asks for evidence. It does not say the water is dangerous, only that the claim needs a test.

items.p: Explain in your own words why the stomach does not burn itself.
items.a: The wall is covered with a thick coat of mucus that holds bicarbonate, a base. The acid is used up as it creeps through, so the wall stays near neutral. The cells of the wall also live only a few days and are replaced all the time.
items.why: A strong answer names the mucus, the bicarbonate and the quick renewal of cells.

items.p: A friend says: 'Acids are bad and bases are good, so I should take an antacid after every meal.'

views.says: Acids burn, so I want less of them. A base cancels them, so it must be good for me.
The stomach needs its acid to digest and to kill germs. Heartburn that comes often needs a check, and not only a tablet.
I would try smaller meals and not lying down right after eating, and keep antacids for the odd time.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What would you want to find out first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason using what we know about stomach acid and antacids, and says what to find out, such as how often the heartburn happens.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. A strong answer shows that the child can weigh a claim, and knows that acid is not simply bad.

items.p: Draw a dye ladder of five cups that shows how the colour fades when every step is ten times weaker.
items.a: Five cups in a row, each with a colour much paler than the one before, with a label such as 1 in 10, 1 in 100, 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 10,000 under them.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the colour getting very pale quickly, and labels each cup with how many times weaker it is.

items.p: Why does Helicobacter pylori make ammonia?
opts: To make a base around herself that protects her from acid
To eat the stomach wall
To make the stomach more acidic
items.why: Ammonia is a base. The bacterium breaks down urea into ammonia, and the ammonia makes a little cloud of neutral liquid around her. It protects her from the acid.

items.p: A bacterium can live in the stomach even though the stomach holds a strong acid.
items.why: True. Helicobacter pylori lives in the mucus and makes ammonia, a base, around herself. Other microbes grow in acid too, such as the bacteria in curd.

items.p: A glass with 2 tablespoons of vinegar needs 3 scoops of cooking soda to neutralise it. How many scoops would you expect for 4 tablespoons of the same vinegar?
items.why: Twice as much acid needs about twice as much base, so 3 times 2 is 6 scoops. Your real number may differ a little.

worksheets.title: Right place, not the biggest number (challenge)

items.p: A dyer's vat reads pH 8 but a good vat reads pH 10. A helper says to pour in a hundred times more lime. Explain why testing a small cup first is wiser.
items.a: The strip shows how far apart the vats are, but not how much lime a big vat needs. Too much lime can push the vat past the right place and stop the tiny living beings in it from working. A small cup test lets us add lime a spoon at a time and read the pH each time, without risking the whole vat.
items.why: A strong answer says that the number does not give the amount, that too much is also wrong, and that a small test is cheap and safe.

items.p: How many times more hydrogen ions does stomach acid at pH 2 have than blood at pH 7.4?
opts: About 250,000 times
About 5 times
About 54 times
items.why: From pH 7.4 down to pH 2 is 5.4 steps. Each step is ten times, so 5 steps make 100,000, and the extra 0.4 of a step makes about two and a half times more. The answer is about 250,000.

items.p: For decades, doctors believed that no bacterium could live in the stomach's acid. A young doctor says she has found one.

views.says: Stomach acid kills germs. This has been taught for many years. Your slides must be dirty.
I have seen the bacteria in many patients and grown them in dishes. Please look at my slides and try the test yourself.

views.who: A patient with an ulcer (an imagined view)
views.says: I do not mind who is right. I want the treatment that stops my ulcer coming back.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer weighs the old belief and the new evidence, says what a good test would be, such as curing patients with antibiotics, and is open to changing its mind.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. A strong answer shows that an old belief can be wrong, and that evidence must decide.

items.p: Cooking soda and a strip of antacid tablets cost about the same. How would you test which one neutralises more acid for the money? Say what you keep the same and what you count.
items.a: I would put the same amount of vinegar and cabbage water in two glasses. I would add one scoop at a time, stirring the same time, and count the scoops each powder needs to match a purple target. I would keep the glass, the acid and the stirring the same. Then I would work out the cost of the scoops that each one used.
items.why: A strong answer keeps the acid, the scoop and the stirring the same, counts scoops to the target colour, and then compares the cost.

items.p: Taking far more antacid than needed is always better, because more base uses up more acid.
items.why: False. Once the stomach acid is used up, more base only adds to the base. The stomach also needs some acid to digest food and kill germs, and too much antacid can upset the stomach.

items.p: The pancreas pours a base called ____ into the small intestine to neutralise acid from the stomach.
a: bicarbonate
items.why: The bicarbonate neutralises the acid that leaves the stomach, so that the enzymes of the small intestine can work at a near-neutral pH.

items.p: Match each pair of liquids to how many times more hydrogen ions the first has.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Count the steps between the two numbers, and multiply ten by itself that many times. One step is 10, two steps are 100, three are 1,000 and four are 10,000.

items.p: Put these steps in the right order for how an antacid tablet works in the stomach.
a: You chew a tablet and swallow it
The tablet dissolves in the stomach acid
The base reacts with hydrogen ions and makes water and a salt
The pH in the stomach rises
The stomach makes more acid, and the effect wears off
items.why: The tablet must dissolve before the base can react. The relief fades because the stomach keeps making acid.

items.p: Draw the stomach as an acid room, the small intestine as a near-neutral room and the bicarbonate that comes between them.
items.a: A drawing with a strongly coloured stomach, a pale intestine, and an arrow from the pancreas carrying bicarbonate into the start of the intestine.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the pancreas adding bicarbonate between the two rooms, so that the pH changes from about 2 to about 7.

items.p: Why should cabbage water not be used alone to decide if a liquid is safe to drink?
opts: The colour is only a rough guide and says nothing about whether a liquid is harmful
Cabbage water is always purple
Cabbage water only works on fruit
items.why: An indicator tells only about the pH, and only roughly. Many harmful liquids have a pH near 7. Never taste or drink something because of its colour.

items.p: Sort each statement by how sure scientists are.
items: Strong stomach acid evolved because our ancestors ate old meat
Why most people with Helicobacter pylori never get an ulcer
Blood is held between pH 7.35 and 7.45
items.a: as given
items.why: What the stomach acid is and what blood pH is have been measured many times. The old-meat idea was suggested in 2015 and is not settled. Why most carriers never get an ulcer is still being studied.

items.p: Hydrogen ions burn the food pipe and also power your cells. Write two sentences about what this tells you about calling things good or bad.
items.a: The same thing can do harm in one place and good in another. Hydrogen ions burn the food pipe but they also make the energy that cells use. So it may be better to ask where and how much, than to ask whether something is good or bad.
items.why: A strong answer says that the same thing can be harmful or useful depending on where it is and how much there is.

items.p: In a dye ladder, the colour was easy to see in cup 3 but gone in cup 4. How many times weaker is cup 3 than cup 0?
items.why: Cup 3 is three steps from cup 0. 10 times 10 times 10 is 1,000.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Toothpaste, cooking soda, lemon juice, milk of magnesia.
items.a: Lemon juice, because it is an acid. The other three hold bases.
items.why: Toothpaste usually holds a base such as a carbonate, cooking soda is sodium bicarbonate, and milk of magnesia is magnesium hydroxide. Lemon juice is an acid.

items.p: If you cannot see any colour in the last cup of a dye ladder, the dye is gone.
items.why: False. Nothing is lost when you dilute. The dye is spread out so thinly that you cannot see it. Weak things can still be there.

items.p: A friend says: 'The stomach is tough, so acid cannot hurt it.' Use what you know to show your friend what is missing.
items.a: The stomach is not safe because it is tough. It has a thick coat of mucus that holds a base, so the acid is used up before it reaches the wall. Its cells also live only a few days and are always replaced. If the coat is damaged, acid can reach the cells and make an ulcer.
items.why: A strong answer says that the stomach is protected by mucus, a base and the quick replacement of cells.

opts: How many free hydrogen ions a watery liquid holds
How hot a liquid is
How thick a liquid is
quiz.why: pH counts the free hydrogen ions in a watery liquid. A low pH means many, and a high pH means few. It does not measure heat or thickness.

quiz.p: A liquid has a pH of 9. What is it?
opts: A weak base
A strong acid
Neutral
quiz.why: Numbers above 7 are bases. Nine is a little above neutral, so it is a weak base, like soapy water.

quiz.p: Liquid A has a pH of 3 and liquid B has a pH of 4. Which statement is true?
opts: A has 10 times as many hydrogen ions as B
A has 3 times as many as B
A and B are almost the same
quiz.why: The scale goes in tenfold steps. A is one step lower, so it has ten times as many hydrogen ions. Seeing them as almost the same is a common mistake.

quiz.p: Which of these gives the most exact reading of pH?
opts: A pH meter
Cabbage water
Tasting the liquid
quiz.why: A pH meter reads to a hundredth of a step. Cabbage water gives only a rough colour. Tasting is never safe, because many strong acids and bases burn.

quiz.p: The middle of the stomach is at about pH 2, but the layer touching the wall is near pH 7. Why?
opts: The mucus holds bicarbonate, which uses up acid before it reaches the wall
The wall makes more acid than the middle
The food neutralises the wall
quiz.why: Mucus traps bicarbonate, a base. It neutralises acid as it creeps through, so the wall stays close to neutral.

opts: Acid splashing up into the food pipe, which has no mucus shield
A pain in the heart muscle
Food that is too hot
quiz.why: Heartburn happens in the food pipe, not the heart. The food pipe has no mucus shield, so stomach acid burns it.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT an antacid?
opts: Table salt
Cooking soda
Magnesium hydroxide
quiz.why: An antacid must be a base. Cooking soda and magnesium hydroxide are bases. Table salt is neutral, and it did nothing in the Antacid Showdown.

quiz.p: In a fair test of antacids, what must stay the same?
opts: The amount of acid, the size of the scoop and the stirring
The kind of powder
The number of scoops
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing, which here is the powder. Everything else stays the same, so that any difference comes from the powder.

quiz.p: Blood stays near pH 7.4 while the stomach is at pH 2. What does this show?
opts: Different parts of the body are held at different pH for their jobs
The body made a mistake
Blood is more acidic than the stomach
quiz.why: Each part of the body needs its own pH. The stomach's acid does a digesting job, and the blood's narrow range keeps cells working.

quiz.p: Doctors believed no bacterium could live in stomach acid. Which finding showed they were wrong?
opts: Helicobacter pylori was found living in the stomach, and antibiotics cured ulcers
Antacids cured every ulcer
Taking away spicy food made every ulcer vanish
quiz.why: A bacterium was found living in the stomach, and killing it with antibiotics cured ulcers for good. Antacids and plain food changes did not.

quiz.p: A change from pH 6 to pH 5 means ten times as many hydrogen ions.
quiz.why: True. One step down the scale is ten times as many hydrogen ions. A small change in the number is a large change in the liquid.

quiz.p: An antacid is a ____ (acid or base).
a: base
quiz.why: An antacid is a base. It reacts with stomach acid and uses some of it up.

Farmers test soil with pH paper and spread lime on soil that is too acidic.
Swimming pool workers test the water's pH and keep it near neutral, so that eyes do not sting.
Bakers and cooks use cooking soda, a base, to cancel the sourness in batters.
Dyers keep indigo vats at the right pH so that the dye works.
Toothpaste holds a base that helps to cancel the acid made by bacteria on teeth.
Doctors test blood and urine pH to find out whether the lungs and kidneys are working.
Scientists check the pH of rivers and the sea to see whether the water is changing.

open_questions.q: Why do most people who carry Helicobacter pylori never get an ulcer?
open_questions.why_open: About half of all people carry the bacterium, but only one in ten or fewer gets an ulcer. Scientists are comparing the bacterium's strains, people's genes and diets, and have no full answer.

open_questions.q: Why are human stomachs as acidic as a vulture's?
open_questions.why_open: One idea says our ancestors ate old meat. Others say the acid helps digestion or guards against the many microbes on all food. No one has found a way to test the ideas on ancestors who lived long ago.

open_questions.q: How safe is it to take strong acid-reducing medicines for many years?
open_questions.why_open: These medicines help many people. Some studies link long use to other problems, such as weaker bones, but it is hard to tell whether the medicine or the illness caused the problem.

open_questions.q: Did the first living cells begin where a difference in pH already existed, such as at warm vents on the sea floor?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think a pH difference across thin rock walls could have powered the first cells. Others think life began in other places. The vents have been studied, but no one has made life from them.

open_questions.q: How exactly does the gut keep its acid and base rooms in the right places?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know the pumps, hormones and nerves that control the stomach and the pancreas, but they are still working out how the whole system is tuned, and why it fails in some people.

When someone burps after a fizzy drink, ask: what do you think the gas is, and where did it come from?

Show a lemon and ask: if one pH step is ten times, how many times stronger than water is this?
Ask: why does your stomach not burn itself?
When someone says they have heartburn, ask: what is happening in their body, and how could a tablet help?
Ask: if a drink looks clear, can you tell if it is an acid or a base? How would you find out?
Ask: why does tea taste different with a squeeze of lemon, and what do you think the lemon does to the colour?

maths.problem: Lemon juice has a pH of 2 and a drink has a pH of 5. How many times as many hydrogen ions does the lemon juice have?
maths.explain: From pH 5 down to pH 2 is three steps. Each step is ten times, so 10 times 10 times 10 is 1,000.
maths.context: In the Ten-Times Ladder and the pH Ladder, you meet the idea that every pH step is ten times.
maths.why_maths: The pH scale multiplies by ten at each step. Powers of ten tell you how big a difference in pH really is.

maths.problem: In a dye ladder, each cup holds ten times less colour than the one before. The colour in cup 6 is how many times weaker than in cup 0?
maths.explain: Six steps of ten is 10 times 10 times 10 times 10 times 10 times 10. That is one million.
maths.context: In the Ten-Times Ladder, you make a colour ten times weaker, step by step, in a row of cups.
maths.why_maths: Each step multiplies by ten, so the numbers grow very fast. Big numbers help to show why the last cup looks like plain water.

maths.problem: Ritu, a girl in Class 4 in Pune, needs 3 scoops of cooking soda for a glass of acid. A strip of 10 antacid tablets costs 30 rupees, and she needs 4 tablets for the same glass. A scoop of cooking soda costs about 20 paise. Which is cheaper for the same glass, and by how many times? (These prices are made up.)
maths.explain: 3 scoops of soda cost 3 times 20 paise, which is 60 paise. 4 tablets cost 4 times 3 rupees, which is 12 rupees, or 1,200 paise. 1,200 divided by 60 is 20. The tablets are made to be safe and handy, which is part of what you pay for.
maths.context: In the Antacid Showdown, you count the scoops of each powder it takes to neutralise the same glass of acid.
maths.why_maths: Counting the scoops and comparing the prices tells you which powder does the job for less money. It is a ratio.

maths.problem: Mira makes curd from warm milk. The pH is 6.6 at the start, 6.0 after 2 hours, 5.2 after 4 hours, 4.6 after 6 hours and 4.4 after 8 hours. In which 2-hour stretch did the pH fall the most? What does it say about the bacteria? (These numbers are made up from typical results.)
maths.answer: Between 2 and 4 hours, when it fell by 0.8. The falls were 0.6, 0.8, 0.6 and 0.2.
maths.explain: The falls are 6.6 minus 6.0 is 0.6, 6.0 minus 5.2 is 0.8, 5.2 minus 4.6 is 0.6 and 4.6 minus 4.4 is 0.2. The bacteria make acid, and as the acid builds up the bacteria slow down, so the fall gets smaller at the end.
maths.context: The acid in curd comes from bacteria. A pH strip can follow the milk turning to curd over a day.
maths.why_maths: A list of readings hides a pattern. Taking the difference between each pair of readings shows when the change was fastest.

maths.problem: Suppose the cells of the stomach lining are replaced about every 4 days. About how many times are they replaced in a year of 365 days?
maths.explain: 365 is close to 360. 360 divided by 4 is 90. So the lining is made new about 90 times a year. A good estimate is enough here.
maths.context: The stomach protects itself with a coat of mucus and with cells that are replaced every few days.
maths.why_maths: An estimate shows how much work the body does all the time to keep the stomach whole, without doing the exact sum.

maths.problem: Put these liquids in order, from the most acidic to the least acidic: curd 4.4, tomato juice 4.2, coffee 5.0, lemon juice 2.2, milk 6.6.
maths.answer: Lemon juice 2.2, tomato juice 4.2, curd 4.4, coffee 5.0, milk 6.6.
maths.explain: The lowest pH is the most acidic. 2.2 is the smallest, then 4.2, then 4.4, then 5.0, and 6.6 is the largest.
maths.context: In the pH Strip Survey, you test liquids and put them in order by their pH.
maths.why_maths: Comparing decimals lets you put the liquids in order, and tells you which is most acidic without a guess.

maths.problem: A dye ladder has 10,000 parts of colour in cup 0. Each cup after it holds a tenth of the one before. Write the number of parts in cups 0 to 4. In which cup does it first fall below 1 part?
maths.answer: 10,000, 1,000, 100, 10 and 1. It falls below 1 part in cup 5.
maths.explain: Dividing by 10 each time gives 10,000, then 1,000, then 100, then 10, then 1 in cup 4. In cup 5 there is only one tenth of a part.
maths.context: In the Ten-Times Ladder, each cup holds a tenth of the colour in the cup before.
maths.why_maths: A number pattern that divides by ten each time shows how a ladder like the pH scale behaves, and when a colour would fade completely.

how_we_found_out.story: For many decades, doctors believed that no bacterium could live in the strong acid of the stomach. They also believed that ulcers, the sore patches in the stomach wall, came from stress, spicy food and too much acid. Patients were told to rest and take antacids. The ulcers kept coming back. In 1979, Robin Warren, a pathologist in Perth, Australia, noticed curved bacteria in stomach samples. In 1981 a young doctor, Barry Marshall, began working with him. In 1982 a dish of stomach samples was left in the warm cupboard over a long Easter weekend, and the slow-growing bacteria finally showed up. Many doctors still did not believe them. So in 1984, Marshall drank a dish of the bacteria. Within days he felt ill, and a camera tube showed that his stomach wall was inflamed. Antibiotics cured him, and later cured many patients. Marshall and Warren shared the Nobel Prize in 2005.
how_we_found_out.who: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren, doctors in Perth, Australia
how_we_found_out.when: 1979 to 1984, and the Nobel Prize in 2005
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Doctors believed that stomach acid kills all bacteria, so ulcers had to come from stress, spicy food and too much acid. Marshall and Warren showed that a bacterium lives in the stomach and causes most ulcers, and that antibiotics cure them.
